questions.prompt: What does it mean for the REST API to be "stateless"?
options: Each request is self-contained and the server retains no memory of previous requests
The API never returns an error
The API only supports read operations
The server stores a session cookie for each logged-in user
questions.explain: Statelessness means every REST call must carry everything the server needs, including authentication, because the server doesn't remember earlier calls.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes a stateful, cookie-based session model — the opposite of what 'stateless' means. Salesforce's REST API carries authentication on every single call via a bearer token instead of relying on a server-side session.

questions.prompt: A company needs to insert 2 million new Lead records into Salesforce as part of a one-time migration. Which API is the right fit, and why?
options: Bulk API 2.0, because it's purpose-built for high-volume asynchronous data loads rather than many single-record calls
The REST API, looping one POST call per record
The Streaming API, since it pushes records in real time
The Metadata API, since Leads are a standard object
questions.explain: Bulk API 2.0's asynchronous job model is designed exactly for this volume; looping single REST calls would be slow and likely hit API limits.

questions.prompt: Match each API family to the one-sentence job this course gives it.
right: Deploying and retrieving org configuration, not application data
Real-time single/few-record CRUD and queries, JSON-based
XML/WSDL-based, used by legacy enterprise integrations
questions.explain: REST is the JSON-based default for everyday real-time CRUD; SOAP is the XML/WSDL legacy option; Bulk API 2.0 handles large asynchronous loads; Metadata API moves org configuration rather than data.

questions.prompt: An integration vendor builds a tool that must work against any Salesforce org without regenerating code when a customer's org schema changes. Which SOAP WSDL should it use, and why?
options: The Enterprise WSDL, because it is strongly typed
The Partner WSDL, because it is generic and loosely typed, working against any org without regeneration
Either WSDL works identically for this purpose
Neither; SOAP cannot be used generically across orgs
questions.explain: The Partner WSDL is deliberately generic so the same client code works unmodified against any org's schema, unlike the Enterprise WSDL which must be regenerated per org.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ WSDL is generated specifically for one org's current schema and must be regenerated if that schema changes.
questions.explain: The Enterprise WSDL bakes in one org's specific custom objects and fields as strongly typed elements, unlike the generic Partner WSDL.

questions.prompt: What is the key practical difference between Bulk API 1.0 and Bulk API 2.0?
options: Bulk API 2.0 is a simpler, pure-REST API where Salesforce manages batching automatically
Bulk API 1.0 only supports queries, never inserts
Bulk API 2.0 requires SOAP
There is no real difference between them
questions.explain: Bulk API 2.0 simplified the model so Salesforce handles optimal batching internally, instead of the caller managing batches manually as in 1.0.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Composite API, GraphQL API, and Streaming API, per this course.
options: Composite API combines multiple REST sub-requests into a single HTTP call
GraphQL API lets a client request an exact, often deeply nested data shape in one round trip
Streaming API is pull-based, requiring the client to repeatedly ask for updates
Change Data Capture is one of the real forms the Streaming API family takes
GraphQL API replaces the need for the REST API entirely
questions.explain: Composite reduces round trips for chained operations, GraphQL lets a client ask for an exact nested shape, and CDC is one of Streaming's real forms (alongside PushTopics and Platform Events) — Streaming is push-based, not pull-based, and GraphQL complements rather than replaces REST.

questions.prompt: Put these five stages of a Bulk API 2.0 job's lifecycle in the correct order.
items: Create the ingest job, specifying the object and operation
Upload CSV data to the job
Close the job by signaling upload is complete
Poll the job until it reaches JobComplete
questions.explain: Every Bulk API 2.0 ingest job follows this same five-stage sequence: create, upload, close, poll, retrieve.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the OAuth flow used for fully automated, server-to-server integrations with no user present to approve access is called the ________ flow.
questions.explain: The JWT Bearer flow signs a JWT assertion with a private key and exchanges it directly for an access token, with no browser redirect or user approval needed.

questions.prompt: A nightly, fully automated job syncs inventory data into Salesforce with no human present. Which OAuth flow fits, per this course?
options: The Web Server (Authorization Code) flow
The JWT Bearer flow
The Device Flow
The legacy Username-Password flow, since it's Salesforce's current recommendation
questions.explain: The JWT Bearer flow is built exactly for server-to-server integrations with no user in the loop; the Username-Password flow is legacy and being retired, not recommended.

questions.prompt: As of 2026, what changed regarding how new OAuth client apps get registered in Salesforce?
options: Nothing changed; Connected Apps remain the only option
Salesforce disabled creating new Connected Apps across all orgs, recommending External Client Apps (ECAs) instead — existing Connected Apps keep working
OAuth itself was removed in favor of raw API keys
Only sandboxes can still create Connected Apps
questions.explain: Winter '26 and Spring '26 extended a block on new Connected App creation to all orgs, with External Client Apps as the new recommended registration object; existing Connected Apps were not deprecated.

questions.prompt: Match each REST CRUD operation to its typical success HTTP status code.
questions.explain: Create returns 201 Created, read returns 200 OK, and both update and delete return 204 No Content with an empty body.

questions.prompt: An integration needs to sync Accounts from an external HR system that has its own identifiers, without first looking up each Account's Salesforce ID. Which REST operation fits?
options: A plain PATCH update by Salesforce record ID
Upsert by external ID field, e.g. PATCH /sobjects/Account/{externalIdField}/{value}
A DELETE followed by a POST
A SOSL search
questions.explain: Upsert matches on a designated external ID field, inserting if no match exists or updating if one does, avoiding the need to already know the Salesforce ID.

questions.prompt: A /query call returns a response with "done": false and a nextRecordsUrl. What should the client do?
options: Stop, since false means the query failed
Call the nextRecordsUrl to retrieve the next batch of matching records
Re-run the exact same original query
Switch to SOSL instead
questions.explain: done: false means more matching records exist beyond this batch, and nextRecordsUrl is exactly how a client continues paging through them.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a full-text search across multiple Salesforce object types in one call is run through the ________ resource, using SOSL rather than SOQL.
questions.explain: /search runs a SOSL query, which can match across several object types in one call, unlike /query's single-object SOQL.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about REST API error handling, per this course.
options: Error response bodies are always a JSON array, even for a single error
A 401 with errorCode INVALID_SESSION_ID should be fixed by refreshing the token and retrying once
A 400 with errorCode REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING should be retried immediately and repeatedly with the same payload
A transient 500 error is a reasonable candidate for retry with backoff
HTTP status codes alone, without errorCode, always tell you exactly what went wrong
questions.explain: Errors always arrive as a JSON array; a 401/INVALID_SESSION_ID calls for a token refresh and single retry; a transient 500 is a good retry-with-backoff candidate. A 400/REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING should never be blindly retried unchanged, and errorCode — not just the status code — is what pins down the specific cause.

questions.prompt: Why do Postman environment variables like {{access_token}} matter specifically for Salesforce API testing?
options: They let you update an expiring access token in one place instead of across every saved request
They are required by Salesforce to authenticate any request
They replace the need for an Authorization header entirely
They only work with the SOAP API
questions.explain: Since access tokens expire, centralizing the value in an environment variable means updating it once instead of hunting through every saved request.

questions.prompt: What is Salesforce Connect, as defined in this course?
options: A feature that displays and queries data living in an external system live, via callout, without copying it into Salesforce
A high-volume asynchronous data-loading API
A real-time push notification API family
A tool for combining several REST sub-requests into one call
questions.explain: Salesforce Connect's defining feature is fetching external data live via callout rather than storing a copy inside Salesforce.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Bulk API 2.0, not Salesforce Connect — Bulk API 2.0 copies and stores data inside Salesforce at volume, while Salesforce Connect's entire point is never copying the external data in at all.

questions.prompt: An org's calls start failing with 403 Forbidden and errorCode REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED partway through the day. What does this mean?
options: The org has exhausted its rolling 24-hour API request allocation
The org's data storage is full
The access token format is invalid
The SOQL query syntax is wrong
questions.explain: REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED paired with 403 specifically signals the org's API request allocation for its current rolling window has been used up.

questions.prompt: Put these four Bulk API 2.0 ingest job HTTP calls in the order they're made, from creating the job to closing it for processing.
items: PATCH /services/data/v61.0/jobs/ingest/{id} with state: UploadComplete (close the job)
questions.explain: The job is created with a POST, data is uploaded with a PUT, the job is closed (queuing it for processing) with a PATCH setting state to UploadComplete, and then the client polls its status with a GET until it reaches JobComplete.

questions.prompt: Match each Composite API form to what it's actually built for.
right: Flat bulk CRUD on a list of same-type records, up to 200 in one call
Independent sub-requests grouped into one call, with no cross-referencing
The most capable form, for complex multi-object transactional graphs
Chained sub-requests (up to 25) that can reference each other's results via referenceId
questions.explain: /composite supports cross-referencing between up to 25 chained sub-requests; /composite/batch groups independent calls with no cross-referencing; /composite/sobjects (sObject Collections) handles flat bulk CRUD; /composite/graph is the most capable form for complex multi-object graphs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Composite Graph supports up to ________ nodes in a single payload, per developer.salesforce.com's verified current limits.
questions.explain: Composite Graph's verified limits include up to 500 nodes per payload, up to 75 graphs per payload, and a maximum graph depth of 15.

questions.prompt: Why is an external object (suffixed __x) fundamentally different from a standard or custom object, even though it can appear in list views and reports the same way?
options: It's backed by live callouts to an external system instead of rows stored inside Salesforce
It can only be created through the SOAP API
It cannot be queried with SOQL at all
It is always read-only and never editable through any API
questions.explain: External objects look and behave like normal objects in the UI, but every query against one triggers a live callout to the external system rather than reading stored Salesforce data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: this course verified that Spring '26 corresponds to Salesforce API version ________.
questions.explain: Spring '26 is API version 66.0, verified against Salesforce's own documentation — roughly three new version numbers appear every year across the Spring, Summer, and Winter releases.

questions.prompt: In the Northstar Supply Co. practice project, select every true statement about the API choices made.
options: A /composite request was used for 6 new Contacts because Bulk API 2.0's job overhead doesn't pay for itself at that small a scale
allOrNone was set to true so the batch would either fully succeed or fully fail, not partially commit
If the batch instead had 40,000 records, the project should switch to the Bulk API 2.0 job lifecycle
The Account's ID had to be looked up first because the new Contacts needed a valid AccountId to link to
Bulk API 2.0 was used from the start because it's always the superior choice regardless of volume
questions.explain: The project deliberately chose /composite for a small batch, used allOrNone for transactional safety, would switch to Bulk API 2.0 at real volume, and looked up the Account ID first to link new Contacts — Bulk API 2.0 is not universally superior, it earns its overhead specifically at scale.

questions.prompt: A company needs to deploy 30 new custom fields from a sandbox into production. Which API handles this, per this course's decision framework?
options: Bulk API 2.0, treating each field as a record
The REST API, creating each field via /sobjects
The Metadata API, since this moves configuration, not application data
The Streaming API
questions.explain: Deploying configuration like custom fields is categorically Metadata API's job, distinct from every other API in this course which moves application data.

questions.prompt: Match each security concept to what it actually protects against, per this course.
right: Restricting where a login or API call is allowed to originate from
Limiting a compromised token's blast radius to only what its scope allows
Assuming a payload is safe just because it arrived through an authenticated channel
Keeping secrets out of code so a compromised one can be rotated without a deployment
questions.explain: Least privilege limits a compromised token's blast radius; Named Credentials keep secrets out of code; Trusted IP Ranges restrict where calls can originate; and validating inbound data guards against the mistake of trusting a payload just because the channel was authenticated.

questions.prompt: What specific security improvement do External Client Apps (ECAs) offer over classic Connected Apps, per this course?
options: They separate an app's identity from its policies (scopes, IP ranges, session behavior), making access easier to audit and tighten
They remove the need for any OAuth scope at all
They make every integration automatically compliant with GDPR
They are purely a rebrand with no functional difference
questions.explain: ECAs give admins a cleaner separation between an app's core registration and the policies governing its access, making it easier to audit and adjust without touching the app's identity.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference this course draws between Workbench and Postman?
options: Workbench is purpose-built around Salesforce specifically, while Postman is a general-purpose API client usable against any API
Postman only works with SOAP, and Workbench only works with REST
They are the exact same tool under two different names
Workbench requires no authentication at all
questions.explain: Workbench is a free, Salesforce-specific tool for ad hoc queries and REST calls, while Postman is a general-purpose client not tied to Salesforce at all — both are referenced by name only in this course, never screenshotted.

questions.prompt: Put these four steps, from this course's final lesson, in the order you'd use them to investigate an unfamiliar integration with no documentation of its own.
items: Check developer.salesforce.com for the authoritative, version-specific behavior of the APIs involved
Use Workbench to run ad hoc SOQL queries or REST calls and see what the integration is actually touching
Call GET /services/data/ to confirm which API versions the org currently supports
Call GET /services/data/v61.0/limits to check whether the org is near any relevant allocation
questions.explain: Starting from authoritative documentation, then probing with an independent tool like Workbench, then confirming the org's actual supported versions and remaining limits, moves from general understanding to the specific, current facts about that org — replacing guesswork with verified facts at each step.
